title: Energy, Energy Transfer & General Energy Analysis

problems.title: Kinetic energy of a car
problems.scenario:
A **1200 kg** car travels at **25 m/s**.

Find its **kinetic energy** in kJ.
hints: $KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mV^2$ — the result is in joules.
Divide by 1000 to convert J → kJ.
problems.solution:
Apply the kinetic-energy formula:

$$KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mV^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(1200)(25)^2 = 0.5 \times 1200 \times 625 = 375\,000\ \text{J} = 375\ \text{kJ}$$

Note it scales with the *square* of speed: doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy.

problems.title: Potential energy lift
problems.scenario:
A crane raises a **50 kg** load by **8.0 m**. Take $g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Find the gain in **potential energy** in kJ.
hints: $PE = mgz$ — in joules.
Convert J → kJ by dividing by 1000.
problems.solution:
$$PE = mgz = 50 \times 9.81 \times 8.0 = 3924\ \text{J} = 3.924\ \text{kJ}$$

This is the minimum work the crane must do against gravity (ignoring friction and acceleration).

problems.title: Energy from an electric heater
problems.scenario:
A **2000 W** electric heater runs for **15 minutes**.

How much **electrical energy** does it consume, in kJ?
hints: Energy = power × time. Watts × seconds = joules.
Convert 15 min to seconds first: $15 \times 60 = 900\ \text{s}$.
problems.solution:
Electrical work is power multiplied by the running time:

$$W_e = \dot W_e\,\Delta t = 2000\ \text{W} \times (15 \times 60)\ \text{s} = 2000 \times 900 = 1\,800\,000\ \text{J} = 1800\ \text{kJ}$$

Keep time in **seconds** so that W·s = J.

problems.title: Ideal pumping power
problems.scenario:
A pump raises water at $\dot m = 20\ \text{kg/s}$ to a reservoir **15 m** higher, with negligible change in pressure and velocity. Take $g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Find the **ideal (minimum) power** required, in kW.
hints: The only mechanical-energy change here is potential energy.
$\dot W = \dot m\,\Delta e_{mech} = \dot m\,g\,\Delta z$.
Result is in watts — divide by 1000 for kW.
problems.solution:
With pressure and velocity unchanged, the pump only adds potential energy to the flow:

$$\dot W = \dot m\,g\,\Delta z = 20 \times 9.81 \times 15 = 2943\ \text{W} = 2.943\ \text{kW}$$

This is the *ideal* power; a real pump needs more (see the next problem).

problems.title: Pump with efficiency
problems.scenario:
The pump from the previous problem (ideal power **2.943 kW**) has a **mechanical efficiency of 0.75**.

Find the **actual shaft power** that must be supplied, in kW.
hints: Efficiency = useful output ÷ required input.
$\eta_{pump} = \dot W_{ideal}/\dot W_{shaft}$, so rearrange for the input.
$\dot W_{shaft} = \dot W_{ideal}/\eta$.
problems.solution:
The pump efficiency relates the useful (ideal) power to the shaft power supplied:

$$\eta_{pump} = \frac{\dot W_{ideal}}{\dot W_{shaft}} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \dot W_{shaft} = \frac{\dot W_{ideal}}{\eta_{pump}}$$

$$\dot W_{shaft} = \frac{2.943}{0.75} = 3.924\ \text{kW}$$

The extra 0.98 kW is lost to friction and other irreversibilities inside the pump.

problems.title: Available wind power
problems.scenario:
Wind at **10 m/s** blows through a turbine rotor of diameter **50 m**. Air density is $\rho = 1.2\ \text{kg/m}^3$.

Find the **total available power** in the wind passing through the rotor, in kW.
hints: The available power is the kinetic energy flux: $\dot W = \tfrac{1}{2}\dot m V^2$ with $\dot m = \rho A V$.
Combine them: $\dot W = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho A V^3$. Swept area $A = \pi D^2/4$.
problems.solution:
The kinetic energy carried by the wind per unit time uses the mass flow $\dot m = \rho A V$:

$$\dot W = \tfrac{1}{2}\dot m V^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho A V^3$$

The swept area:

$$A = \frac{\pi D^2}{4} = \frac{\pi (50)^2}{4} = 1963.5\ \text{m}^2$$

Then:

$$\dot W = \tfrac{1}{2}(1.2)(1963.5)(10)^3 = 0.5 \times 1.2 \times 1963.5 \times 1000 = 1\,178\,000\ \text{W} \approx 1178\ \text{kW}$$

A real turbine can extract at most 59% of this (the Betz limit), and less in practice.

problems.title: Hydroelectric power output
problems.scenario:
Water falls **90 m** through a hydroelectric plant at $\dot m = 500\ \text{kg/s}$. The combined turbine–generator efficiency is **0.84**. Take $g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Find the **electric power output**, in kW.
hints: First find the ideal power from the drop: $\dot W_{ideal} = \dot m\,g\,\Delta z$.
Then multiply by the efficiency (output = η × input).
$\dot W_{elec} = \eta\,\dot m\,g\,\Delta z$.
problems.solution:
The available mechanical power from the falling water is:

$$\dot W_{ideal} = \dot m\,g\,\Delta z = 500 \times 9.81 \times 90 = 441\,450\ \text{W} = 441.5\ \text{kW}$$

The turbine–generator converts a fraction of it to electricity:

$$\dot W_{elec} = \eta\,\dot W_{ideal} = 0.84 \times 441.5 = 370.8\ \text{kW}$$

problems.title: Combined motor–pump efficiency
problems.scenario:
An electric **motor** (efficiency 0.90) drives a **pump** (efficiency 0.70). The useful mechanical power delivered to the fluid is **4.0 kW**.

Find the **electrical power** drawn from the grid, in kW.
hints: Component efficiencies multiply: $\eta_{overall} = \eta_{motor}\,\eta_{pump}$.
$\dot W_{elec} = \dot W_{useful}/\eta_{overall}$.
$\eta_{overall} = 0.90 \times 0.70 = 0.63$.
problems.solution:
Chain the two devices: electricity → motor → pump → fluid. The overall efficiency is the product:

$$\eta_{overall} = \eta_{motor}\,\eta_{pump} = 0.90 \times 0.70 = 0.63$$

The electrical input needed for 4.0 kW of useful output is:

$$\dot W_{elec} = \frac{\dot W_{useful}}{\eta_{overall}} = \frac{4.0}{0.63} = 6.35\ \text{kW}$$

Losses compound — each stage takes its cut, so the grid must supply far more than the useful 4 kW.

problems.title: Power lost to friction in a pump
problems.scenario:
A pump supplies **20 kW** of shaft power to raise water at $\dot m$ corresponding to $\dot V = 0.030\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}$ to a reservoir **45 m** higher. Take $\rho = 1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$, $g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Find the mechanical power **converted to thermal energy by friction** (i.e., the loss), in kW.
hints: First find the *ideal* (useful) power actually needed to raise the water: $\dot W_{ideal} = \dot m g\Delta z$.
$\dot m = \rho\dot V$.
The loss is simply the gap between what's supplied and what's usefully delivered: $\dot W_{loss} = \dot W_{shaft} - \dot W_{ideal}$.
problems.solution:
The mass flow rate is:

$$\dot m = \rho\dot V = 1000\times0.030 = 30\ \text{kg/s}$$

The *useful* (ideal) power needed to lift this water is:

$$\dot W_{ideal} = \dot m g\Delta z = 30\times9.81\times45 = 13\,244\ \text{W} = 13.24\ \text{kW}$$

The pump is supplied 20 kW of shaft power, but only 13.24 kW does useful work on the water — the rest is dissipated by friction (turbulence, internal losses) and appears as a small temperature rise:

$$\dot W_{loss} = \dot W_{shaft} - \dot W_{ideal} = 20 - 13.24 = 6.76\ \text{kW}$$

problems.title: Pump efficiency with a diameter change
problems.scenario:
An oil pump ($\rho = 860\ \text{kg/m}^3$) draws **44 kW** of electric power and delivers a flow rate of **0.10 m³/s**. The inlet pipe diameter is **8 cm** and the outlet is **12 cm**. The pressure rise across the pump is **500 kPa**, and the motor driving the pump is **90% efficient**. Elevation change is negligible.

Find the **mechanical efficiency of the pump** itself (as a decimal), accounting for the change in kinetic energy caused by the diameter change.
hints: First find the shaft power actually delivered to the pump: $\dot W_{shaft} = \dot W_{elec}\times\eta_{motor}$.
Find inlet/outlet velocities from continuity: $V = \dot V/A$, with $A = \pi D^2/4$. The bigger outlet pipe means the fluid *slows down*.
The fluid's mechanical energy gain per unit mass is $\Delta e = \Delta P/\rho + (V_{out}^2-V_{in}^2)/2$ — note the KE term is *negative* here. Pump efficiency = $\dot m\Delta e / \dot W_{shaft}$.
problems.solution:
**Shaft power into the pump** (after the motor's own losses):

$$\dot W_{shaft} = \dot W_{elec}\times\eta_{motor} = 44\times0.90 = 39.6\ \text{kW}$$

**Velocities from continuity.** Pipe areas: $A_{in} = \pi(0.08)^2/4 = 0.005027\ \text{m}^2$, $A_{out} = \pi(0.12)^2/4 = 0.011310\ \text{m}^2$.

$$V_{in} = \frac{0.10}{0.005027} = 19.89\ \text{m/s}, \qquad V_{out} = \frac{0.10}{0.011310} = 8.84\ \text{m/s}$$

The fluid *decelerates* through the pump since the outlet pipe is wider.

**Mechanical energy gained by the fluid** (pressure rise minus the kinetic-energy loss):

$$\Delta e = \frac{\Delta P}{\rho} + \frac{V_{out}^2-V_{in}^2}{2} = \frac{500\,000}{860} + \frac{8.84^2-19.89^2}{2} = 581.4 - 158.8 = 422.6\ \text{J/kg}$$

With $\dot m = \rho\dot V = 860\times0.10 = 86\ \text{kg/s}$, the useful power delivered to the fluid is:

$$\dot W_{useful} = \dot m\,\Delta e = 86\times422.6 = 36.34\ \text{kW}$$

**Pump efficiency:**

$$\eta_{pump} = \frac{\dot W_{useful}}{\dot W_{shaft}} = \frac{36.34}{39.6} = 0.918$$

The kinetic-energy drop *works against* the pressure rise — ignoring it (a common mistake) would overstate the useful power and thus the efficiency.

problems.title: Elevator with a counterweight
problems.scenario:
A fully loaded elevator cabin has a mass of **800 kg**. Its weight is partially balanced by a **400 kg** counterweight connected over a pulley at the top of the shaft (frictionless, massless cables). The cabin rises at a **constant speed of 1.2 m/s**. Take $g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Find the **minimum power** required from the motor, in kW.
hints: At *constant* speed there's no acceleration, so the motor only needs to overcome the *net* weight difference between the cabin and the counterweight.
The counterweight already balances part of the cabin's weight — the motor only lifts the imbalance.
$\dot W = (m_{cabin} - m_{cw})\,g\,V$.
problems.solution:
Because the cabin moves at **constant speed**, there's no net acceleration — the motor only has to supply the force needed to overcome the weight *not* already balanced by the counterweight:

$$F_{net} = (m_{cabin} - m_{cw})\,g = (800-400)\times9.81 = 3924\ \text{N}$$

Power is force times speed:

$$\dot W = F_{net}\times V = 3924\times1.2 = 4709\ \text{W} = 4.71\ \text{kW}$$

Without the counterweight, the motor would need to lift the *full* 800 kg — nearly double the power. This is exactly why elevators use counterweights: the motor only ever handles the imbalance, not the total load.
